ideas.title: Climb anything
ideas.critique: Dropping the snapping twig and adding a grip budget makes this more honest: the island has never been a place you climb, and edges read off the real meshes are a real mechanic. Everything hangs on the edge finder and the two-point hang being stable. If Lumi jitters on the ledge or slides along the wall, the film turns into the same glitch reel as the stomp takes.

ideas.title: Footprints that tell on you
ideas.critique: Bekker sinkage per soil and foot, plus a thief that is just whoever is hungriest, fixes both weak points from round 1. Reading prints is a real skill. The risk is that the prints come out as shallow bumps that only show at low sun, and that the hungriest friend is the same one every time, which makes the mystery scripted in practice.

ideas.title: The bees and the smoker
ideas.critique: Replacing the hive's pull with an advected scent field removes the scripted shortcut, and herding with a cloud that drifts in the wind is a fresh twin-stick loop. The last swarm of specks the island filmed read as pulsing dots that barely moved. Thousands of boids have to read as bees in flight, or this becomes the same take.

ideas.title: Grass fire
ideas.critique: Rothermel spread on a level-set front, with firebreaks and water feeding the same equation, is a real simulation with tactics, and black ground that stays for days is something to come back to. Most likely the front comes out as an orange contour under emissive cones. The fight is one route to one cottage, so it may play the same every time.

ideas.title: Mirror signals
ideas.critique: A traced sun spot that really reflects and stretches with the angle is good RayMakie material, and the hour deciding where you can reach is a nice rule. But the island's second optics toy in a short span repeats the camera obscura's payoff. The reactions (waking, chasing, a friend flashing back) will almost surely be scripted triggers on a single ray hit.

ideas.title: Frost flowers on the window
ideas.critique: Kobayashi dendrites with six-fold anisotropy are small, well-understood physics that can look exactly right, and frost that grows back over your marks is a lovely persistent touch. It is a quiet toy on a window pane: once seen, there is little goal. A close-up time-lapse of growing crystals is beautiful but may read as a screensaver, not as play on the island.
